description:
Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) 

7 August 2015: Observed a Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) family consisting of what seemed to be a mother and two ducklings foraging and swimming on the far eastern spillway’s lake at the Lake Lewisville Environmental Learning Area (LLELA) in Lewisville, Texas. It appeared that these particular Mallard ducklings had been raised here on site at LLELA as they were still too small to be able to take flight. According to LLELA veteran observers Michael D. Fox and Erin Taylor whom we accompanied on this particular day, this temporary lake had not been filled with water for some time up until the historic spring rains and especially those of May 2015, which filled it up and created a roaring itinerant river. By the time of our visit the river had stopped flowing but the lake remained much to the liking of this Mallard family. The question is: Where are all the other ducklings that were surely part of the larger original brood? LLELA is administered jointly by the US Army Corps of Engineers, the City of Lewisville, Texas, and the University of North Texas.

This is the thumbnail sketch offered for Mallard by All About Birds: “If someone at a park is feeding bread to ducks, chances are there are Mallards in the fray. Perhaps the most familiar of all ducks, Mallards occur throughout North America and Eurasia in ponds and parks as well as wilder wetlands and estuaries. The male’s gleaming green head, gray flanks, and black tail-curl arguably make it the most easily identified duck. Mallards have long been hunted for the table, and almost all domestic ducks come from this species.” If in North America Mallards appear to be everywhere all at once that is because they (nearly) are. Mallards are considered “dabbling ducks” and are a common sight in urban and suburban metropolitan areas across the country including the Dallas-Fort Worth metro area where it is considered to be a “permanent resident” according to the NatureServe range map.

Mallard is a permanent resident of most of the continental United States except for parts of the Southeast and Southwest including the far southern and western reaches of Texas though two-thirds of the state approximately provides either a “non-breeding” and/or “permanent” home for this duck species. The Mallard’s range in the Northeast of the United States has been expanding. On the other hand its once wintering grounds and southernmost range in Central America have contracted and Mallard’s presence there is now considered to be “rare.” Most of Canada is considered a breeding range for Mallard from one coast to the other, and along Canada’s Pacific Coast on toward Alaska’s Aleutian Islands, there Mallard makes a permanent home too. Mallard is also present as a non-breeding resident in parts of the Caribbean as is the case with Cuba. Mexico’s northwest and its northeast provide Mallard with its southernmost range including the Baja California Peninsula, the Pacific Coast including Sonora and Sinaloa, while on the northeast and northcentral regions of the country states like Chihuahua, Durango and Tamaulipas serve a similar purpose for this duck species. One of the names for Mallard in Spanish is “Pato de Collar” (necklace duck).

Because of its North American credentials placing it in Canada, United States, Mexico and the Caribbean, Mallard is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere.

description:
Domestic Duck (Anas platyrhynchos domesticus)

11 August 2014: At the southside (south of Windsor Drive) lake (of the two that exist) at North Lakes Park in Denton, Texas there is a pair of resident Domestic Ducks (Anas platyrhynchos domesticus) who are well known to the park and lake's regulars some of whom are friends of the pair of Domestic Ducks to the point that they visit them regularly and feed them pieces of white bread and what not. This observation documents this pair of resident North Lakes Park Domestic Ducks. They coexist next to the wild aquatic birds (including Double-crested Cormorant, Great Egret, and Great Blue Heron, for example) at this site who come and go at will, but not these two, this pair, who have no intent of leaving the site that's home for all intents and purposes, hence these two are most definitely Domestic Ducks. They own the southside lake at North Lakes Park. Because they reflect the thousands of years old interaction between Human societies and the flora and fauna around them, Domestic Ducks are authentic residents of the Western Hemisphere. North Lakes Park is administered by the City of Denton, Texas.

Source: "Confusing Domestic Ducks (and Hybrids)," All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, photographs, short essay, accessed 11.20.15, http://www.birds.cornell.edu/crows/domducks.htm

Mallard (Anas platyrynchos)

1 October 2014: A small flock of Mallards (Anas platyrynchos) was gathered at the edge of Lake Lewisville at the Little Elm Park in Little Elm, Texas. While wild they were gentle enough to allow us to approach quite close and take some pics of which this observation presents two, male and female portraits. The thumbnail sketch for Mallard at the All About Birds site is succinct: "If someone at a park is feeding bread to ducks, chances are there are Mallards in the fray. Perhaps the most familiar of all ducks, Mallards occur throughout North America and Eurasia in ponds and parks as well as wilder wetlands and estuaries. The male’s gleaming green head, gray flanks, and black tail-curl arguably make it the most easily identified duck. Mallards have long been hunted for the table, and almost all domestic ducks come from this species." Mallards are present throughout North America including the Caribbean and absent in Central and South America. But they are widespread also in Eurasia and as a result are not only resident in the Western Hemisphere but globally making them authentic residents of planet Earth. Little Elm Park is administered by the City of Little Elm, Texas.

Source: "Mallard," All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, range map, photographs, description, resource links, accessed 11.27.15, https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Mallard/id

description:
Green-winged Teal (Anas crecca)

(Anas crecca carolinensis)

7 March 2015: The ever-changing Wetlands Lake at the Clear Creek Natural Heritage Center (CCNHC) in Denton, Texas, offered up this observation during the late winter season. The digital images presented in this observation are of four male Green-winged Teals (Anas crecca) and one female accompanied on their takeoff (sensing our approach) from the lake’s surface by a lone male Blue-winged Teal. Green-winged Teal is a duck species of North America but one that also occurs in Eurasia. The farthest southern extent of their wintering range occurs in southern Mexico and in the Caribbean where it resides during its winter migration in Cuba and other Island nations. The NatureServe range map also appears to indicate that Green-winged Teal occurs as a vagrant on both the Pacific and Atlantic Coasts of several Central American nations. And on the northern edge of South America on the Atlantic Coast of Venezuela there appears to be a small, even tiny, permanent range for Green-winged Teal. If so, this Venezuelan permanent range would constitute its most southern range in the hemisphere. Nearly all of Mexico except for the region associated with the Yucatan Peninsula provides a wintering range for Green-winged Teal, thus it is a duck that people in Mexico observe annually and indicates the flexible capacity to adapt to different altitudes and environments of this species. All the southern half of the United States provides wintering range as well and its single largest permanent range occurs in several US West states including Washington, Oregon, Montana, Idaho, North Dakota, South Dakota, Colorado, Nevada, California and Arizona. This range is spread far apart and is intermittent at points. Where Green-winged Teal does not winter within the United States, it migrates and also claims a breeding range in the region associated with the Great Lakes states of the Upper Midwest and the Northeast and thence all of Canada to the north and Alaska to the northwest and north comprise breeding range for Green-winged Teal. Indeed the northern regions of Alaska and its Arctic Ocean constitute the farthest northern range for Green-winged Teal. Green-winged Teal occurs in the Western Hemisphere (Anas crecca carolinensis) and in Eurasia (Anas crecca crecca). Because of its extensive flight north and south throughout the Americas, Green-winged Teal is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. And indeed this is a species that flies over large parts of the world. The CCNHC is administered by the City of Denton, Texas.

description:
Northern Pintail (Anas acuta) - male & female

Image 1: male
Image 2: male & female in flight
Image 3: 2 males & 1 female in flight
Images 4-6: male

13 February 2016
Village Creek Drying Beds
NW Green Oaks Boulevard/N. Fielder Road
Arlington, Texas

Hundreds if not thousands of ducks and other waterfowl were observed at the site of the Village Creek Drying Beds. They very slowly but surely tend to gently swim away as one approaches on the high berms or lower hiking paths available. A few other folks were out there with their scopes and cameras, another with a set of binoculars and a dog. A single Turkey Vulture flew overhead making high and low turns as it were. Song Sparrows, Red-winged Blackbirds, and Yellow-rumped Warblers were observed on the wooded side opposite the collection of ponds. The ponds were all filled with water and some of them poured over their respective dividing land spaces and thus joined due to the abundance of the liquid. Bonaparte's Gulls, American Coots, Gadwalls, and Northern Shovelers were the most common waterfowl on site with lesser numbers of other species including Northern Pintail. The hike around the perimeter of the Village Creek Drying Beds makes for good exercise; it is easily a two-to-three mile loop.

Northern Pintail winters or resides permanently throughout the southern half of the United States, most of Mexico, and nearly all of Central America. Together these vast spaces provide a continental wintering haven for this species. Northern Pintail breeds throughout much of Canada from its Atlantic to Pacific coasts, and their northernmost reach is in Alaska, where it also breeds. This duck species also breeds in the Upper Midwest states of the US, and several states in the US West provide a permanent residence. Because of its extensive North American presence, Northern Pintail is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. Village Creek Drying Beds is administered by the City of Arlington, Texas.

description:
This particular duck is problematical...or just annoying.  I was studying a set of about six dark Mallard-type ducks on the water treatment ponds in Asherton, TX (Dimmit County).  At least two of them, maybe four of the six, clearly had double white speculum borders and medium brown base color on the body feathering, and I did not hestitate to mark them down as "Mexican Mallards" in my field journal.  Then I tried to get some pics of at least one of the ducks by digiscoping...and the result on this particular drake seems to show at least a semblance of the diagnostic black basal mark on the bill which would make this a Mottled Duck...but I did NOT see the speculum on this particular duck since it was hidden next to the embankment of the pond.

So, either I had a mixture of Mexican Mallards (observed) and Mottled Duck(s) (one photographed), or some individuals in this set of ducks show some hybrid characters.  I'm leaning on the mixed flock theory here just because I don't want to address the "H" issue.

Interior South Texas has become a confusing area for "Mallard" identification as Mottled Ducks have progressively moved inland to lakes and farm tanks well off the coast, and at the same time, true Mexican Mallards have colonized the entire Rio Grande corridor from West Texas down to the the Lower Rio Grande Valley (e.g. at least to Falcon Dam).  The situation in the zone from about Del Rio down to at least to Laredo and inland a hundred miles is quite confusing...and many birders don't realize how problematic this ID puzzle can be*.  Jeez...

* Here are range maps from eBird sightings for the two species:
Mottled:  http://tinyurl.com/hvs5bc5
Mexican Mallard: http://tinyurl.com/hg44owc
Zoom in to South Texas to see the areas of overlap of these two.

(Addendum: I saw several perfectly good Mottled Ducks (e.g. with very dark body plumage and a narrow single white rear speculum border) the next morning on water bodies just N of Carrizo Springs but was unable to get identifiable images of any of those.)

This morning I studied at least three different pairs of Mottled Ducks on water bodies N of Carrizo Springs, TX.  This drake (and a nearby hen) flew in and landed in a flooded field along FM 1433.  Both had very dark body plumage and a single rear white wing speculum border.  This is the best I could do to get an image of them; the nearby hen fed almost continuously and never raised her head.

See further discussion of this interesting region on an earlier observation in nearby Asherton, TX:
http://www.inaturalist.org/observations/2792934

9 April 2016 
Centennial Park
Irving, Dallas County, Texas

A group of one female, a male, and one duckling were sitting along the Mirror Lake. The male was very attentive to all sounds and frequently kept his head high and neck extended. The mother rarely looked around, and instead she tucked her head away. The duckling did the same, but it also preened its feathers, and looked around. However, the duckling never seemed on the alert. Is the male protecting his family with this behavior, or is he simply observing his environment. Eventually, the male relaxed too.

Something peaked all of the ducks interest, because all 3 of them sat up and quacked. A few moments later, a large duck flew down and landed near the duck family. The family waddled over to it and it started squacking. It didnt stay very long until it flew away again. The ducks seemed confused when it left. What is the relationship between this group of birds and the lone duck?

The Ancona comes in Black and White, Blue and White, Chocolate and White, Lavender and White, Silver and White,  Tricolored and solid White. description: Too bad it was so foggy and drizzling that day. The ducks' color would have looked much brighter.

The day we had the fog last week or so I went out to Lake Arlington and found these two Green- Winged Teals. These guys are Green, Gray, Chestnut, with some black, and white, and on the tail they have a beige-yellow kind of color. These are a smaller duck and are not often seen at Lake Arlington. On occasion you might see them but not too often. I saw one last year but didn't get a good enough picture to share more than an outline. This one is in better detail. I love Green- Winged Teals. They are a beautiful duck and one of the coolest. We have three kinds of teals in this area; we have these and the Blue Winged Teal, and the Cinnamon Teal. These guys are mostly concentrated in the coastal region. Down at the coast like I experienced last winter they gather in the masses on swampy areas and salt marshes. Port Aransas was full of these guys last year. Green- Winged Teals are a dabbling duck which means they don't do far for food. The term "bottoms up" has a whole new meaning if you watch dabbling ducks. They will flip themselves forward and all you can see are their tails. These guys are very destructive with the green eye patch and that gray coat of feathers. They are a very interesting duck and are one of the coolest in my book. The females lack the white streak on the wing and are duller in color. These are two males that were sitting on the bank. I didn't get but two pictures because they flew off before I could get another few. I am very pleased with these photos and was very happy to see these before they flew. They are a beautiful duck to watch while flying. I love birds in flight but sometimes it is nice if you can get a bird to sit still long enough to get a photo or two. I specialize in waterfowl but I do love my tree and ground dwellers. It is just harder to get the tree birds but Waterfowl is my favorite type of bird to photograph because they don't move around too much. That doesn't mean I don't like a good challenge but I just have my preferences that's all but I love all types of birds. It just takes more energy to do tree bird photos which I don't mind at all.

description:
White Rock Lake lower spillway steps.
I was at the fence overlooking the WRL lower spillway steps when I saw this mallard exhibiting behavior new to me.  He would walk up to the top of the incline them swim backwards with his beak under water, swiveling it back and forth rapidly.  Hit the bottom then walk back up and do it all over again.  Turns out there was a lot of tiny silver shad being carried over the edge and down the spillway steps.  All the duck had to do was position its bill and scoop them up, gulp and repeat.  
  Never saw a mallard eat fish before.  Looked it up and Cornell said this about their diet:  "Mallards are generalist foragers and will eat a wide variety of food. They don’t dive, but dabble to feed, tipping forward in the water to eat seeds and aquatic vegetation. They also roam around on the shore and pick at vegetation and prey on the ground. During the breeding season, they eat mainly animal matter including aquatic insect larvae, earthworms, snails and freshwater shrimp. During migration, many Mallards consume largely agricultural seed and grain. In city parks, they readily accept handouts from parkgoers. "  No mention of fish.

description:

12 park duck fight series 
Photo 1:  I was at Sunset Bay when these 2 male mallards suddenly launched into a wild fight.  It set off all the geese honking and went on for several minutes.  They ignored me as I took as many photos as I could of the battle.  Yes, there was a nearby female mallard who looked on and quacked away while it was going on.
Photo 2:  The smaller mallard seemed to be the aggressor. 
Photo 3:  The smaller duck braces himself and goes after the larger duck.  
Photo 4:  The larger duck fights back and uses his body weight to press down on the smaller one.
Photo 5:  The fight got more heated as both ducks are on the offense now.  The female duck is still in the vicinity.
Photo 6:  Smaller duck takes down the larger duck. Larger duck has the curly tail.
Photo 7:  Larger duck manages to get out of the choke hold.  Sure hope that female duck was worth this.  You cannot imagine how loud this fight was with the participants and the crowd of ducks and geese.
Photo 8:  The preferred place to grab hold seems to be the neck.  Here they each have ahold of the others neck.
Photo 9:  Still with the neck holds.  I am not sure what that is supposed to accomplish.
Photo 10:  Finally the bird on the right gains an advantage while the female puts in her 2 cents.
Photo 11:  By this point the smaller duck is clearly winning the battle, which surprised me.  I like how the light is hitting their heads and making one look green and the other blue.
Photo 12:  This is the last in this series of photos.  The larger duck ran off and things settled back down.

description: I don't remember posting these guys and they are so common. These guys are normally migratory but here at Lake Arlington and at some of the other places I frequent they have become so used to handouts from humans that they have given up their migratory instinct and stay at places where they are fed. They are one of the most common ducks and one of the most prettiest. They have a head of green but sometimes can have a head of blue, they have gray scale backs, chestnut breasts, and black and white. They are one of the only ducks that truly make a quack. These guys also have dull yellow bills. The females look a little bit different than the males which I just described. They are a brown and black drab color blend. They also have a blue patch on their wings and they have an orange bill. These guys can be found any day at the lake and are one of my favorites to see. These ducks were the only ones that I would see when I was younger and before I was a birder. For me they were my very first ducks.

description:
White Rock Lake, Sunset Bay
This is a shot I have never published because I was not sure it was appropriate for anywhere.  More of a science shot so appropriate here.  If not, please let me know.  A completely accidental shot.  This duck had some pretty colors from the front and I took some shots of it and it turned around when I took my last shot.  I never saw the dangly parts until processing photos.  And I never saw any mating activity, had just walked up to the area.  I knew what the corkscrew was but not the bulging part.  I sent the shot to the Cornell Lab of Ornithology.  I  got a reply back that said:
"Hi Kala,
Thanks for your patience. 
So that's part of the cloaca that is bulging, and the 'penis' is an extension of that. 
http://scienceblogs.com/notrocketscience/2009/12/22/ballistic-penises-and-corkscrew-vaginas-the-sexual-battles/
Would guess that this male just mated and is in the 2 minute period before the organ retracts.
Wicked cool picture--thanks for sharing!!!
Marc
Marc Devokaitis
Public Information Specialist"

description:
Four Green-winged Teal (Anas crecca), photographed along the banks of Flood Slough at Bedwell Bayfront Park (Menlo Park, CA).  This is one of our smaller ducks, with a rounded head and a small but rotund body.  Its legs are pushed back just a bit too far towards its tail to provide its body with proper support, so it walks about on land with a somewhat exaggerated waddle.  In the water, however, it is as graceful as any of our other ducks.

With both males and females, their small size, rotund bodies, rounded heads, and rather small, narrow, black bills are important field marks.  In addition, the males have a rich, rufous-brown color to their heads that is offset by a green patch over each eye, a black rump, and gray flanks that bear a bright, white vertical stripe at the shoulders.  Both males and females sport a bright, greenish patch on their wings known as the speculum, from which the species derives its common name.

description:
White Rock lake, rushes along banks of Winfrey Point
This was the first time I saw the American black duck.  I'd heard the news, it was such a rare occurrence that birders were coming here from all over the country to see it.  I was walking along the shore hoping to spot it when I accidentily flushed her & her mallard mate out into open water.  Wow, she was so dark, all over.  With her blue speculum that had no white at all.
Now that she was out in the water, she decided to have a bath with lots of splashing.  She had a mate with her, a mallard.  Any offspring will be hybrids.  
After she was done bathing, she rotated her head rapidly, flinging the water drops off.  This species breeds in Canada and winters on the east coast.  Texas is not even on a migration path so they are not supposed to be in this state, ever.  No wonder everyone was showing up to see her.
After she shook the water off, she moved into preening mode.  She didn't seem to mind me as long as I kept my distance.  
She was very particular about where each feather went.  Once one side was done, she started in on the other side.
As she turned while preening, I could see that she was dark everywhere.  So different from female mallards.  She showed the blue speculum often which is good.  That is one of the main things that needs to be photographed to confirm the id.  
Finishing off the bath with a wing clap.  And showing off those beautiful blue feathers outlined in black.  I could not have asked for a better photo opportunity with this rare duck.
She & her mate left the area shortly after this.

description:
White Rock lake, Sunset Bay
7 part behavior series:  Mallard mating behavior
Photo 1:  As I was walking out on the Sunset Bay pier, I heard a loud commotion going on.  Discovered there were two male mallards violently trying to mate with a large domestic mallard mix.  
Photo 2:  Male # 1 grabs her by the back of her head as the weight of the 2 male ducks pushes her body underwater.
Photo 3:  She is almost completely under the water now.  Most of the time, the female is ok after one of these occurances.  However, occasionally, the female will actually drown in the process.  
Photo 4:  She was struggling to keep her head above water.
Photo 5:  Both males are trying to grab her by the back of her (mostly underwater) head.
Photo 6:  She managed to get her head about the water again and was swimming for dry ground as fast as she could.  
Photo 7:  One mallard dropped out of the action and the remaining male pushed her underwater again.  At this point I got distracted by a kingfisher that flew by making a racket.  When I turned my attention back to the ducks, the female had climbed out on the bank and the male was still in the water.  So she was ok.  I went off to pursue the kingfisher.
